listPriors.about: Vote-share points added to the field mean before the lean, each a class of list the final-week polls have missed in one direction in both halves of 2013-2022 (round1/B-list-bias.md; the direction confirmed independently in round1/C-threshold.md and round1/E-context.md). Shrunk 20-40% toward zero. The common lean stays gross: netting it of the Shas miss scored worse out of sample (backtest/v2.mjs). Version 3 (round2/B): the Joint List's +0.4 is superseded by the Arab sector turnout term below (sectorTurnout.replacesPriors) and kept here only so version 2 can be reproduced (model.mjs opts.v2).

forecast.scoring: Score on the official result: per-list absolute seat error of `point`; bloc absolute error of blocs.*.point (version 3: the median of the bloc's simulated total; blocs.*.listSum, the sum of the bloc's list points, is reported beside it, not scored); threshold calls right (`call`, i.e. passes >= 50, and the list passed, or not and it failed); whether the outcome with the highest probability in `majority` occurred. Compare with the two site averages scored the same way.

config.inclusionRule: Every pollster that publishes its sample size and method is averaged, Channel 14 included. Pollsters are included or left out by firm and stated method, never by their results.

withoutVariant.label: Without Channel 14 and i24NEWS
withoutVariant.note: The same average without the polls by Shlomo Filber's firms: Channel 14 (Next Data) and i24NEWS (Direct Polls).

polls.note: Kan did not report Shas or UTJ separately. The listed parties add up to 106, so Shas and UTJ together hold 14 (our arithmetic: 120 − 106).

combined.note: 120 minus the 106 seats Kan listed for everyone else

polls.note: Sep 23 and Sep 28 polls also cited; figures marked date-uncertain are the latest in our register without a date.
Imported from Wikipedia (revision 1381477545). Amcha Yisrael 2.9% (below the threshold) added by hand from the Wikipedia row, 2026-10-23; the import had dropped it.

The final Kan 11 poll (Kantar), published Friday Oct 23 before the blackout; entered by hand 2026-10-24 from Zman Yisrael's live report, ynet's roundup (https://www.ynet.co.il/news/elections2026/article/hy500sxt2mx; sample 1,006, margin 3%, Amcha Yisrael 2.9%) and Haaretz's live blog (sample given there as 1,106; its Democrats figure of 9 makes 121 seats and is a transcription error: Kan's table has 8, and the Eisenkot bloc total of 52 that every source reports requires it). The final Channel 13 poll (the HaMadad consortium), published Friday Oct 23 before the blackout; entered by hand 2026-10-24 from Zman Yisrael's live report and ynet's roundup (https://www.ynet.co.il/news/elections2026/article/hy500sxt2mx; 1,875 respondents, margin 2.3%; Haredi Public 1.3%). Haaretz's live blog gives the sample as 1,084. Not yet on Wikipedia.

partyFile.provenance: CRC party registers 11a–11d (docs/class-11*.md), compiled Oct 4, 2026; ported from Coalition Builder v2 / Party Map v2.
partyFile.bioSource: Each bio names its sources in parentheses.

parties.name: Likud
parties.surplusLine: Surplus: Religious Zionism (signed Oct 6; official, CEC gazette Oct 19)

who.text: Founded Sept 13, 1973 by Begin and Sharon; won power in 1977 with 43 seats.
Netanyahu has led it since 2005 (and 1993–99). The Aug 17, 2026 primary put Eli Cohen first; Netanyahu used reserved slots to move hardliners down.
No written 2026 platform; Likud “does not participate in questionnaires.”

voters.text: Its 2022 voters were 57% traditional, 32% secular, 10% national-religious, 1% Haredi. It won 46.5% of traditional voters and 20% of secular voters.
Strong in periphery cities: Beersheba 42%, Eilat 42%, Ashkelon 40% in 2021.
First-time voters (18–22): 14%, behind Yashar's 16%.

draft.text: Netanyahu revived the Haredi exemption bill as the coalition fell apart; Likud's Sharren Haskel vowed to fight it.

courts.text: Levin, unveiling the overhaul: “We go to the polls, vote, elect, and time after time, people we didn't elect choose for us… That is not democracy.” Aired in August 2026: “We'll wait for the next term, when two-thirds of the Supreme Court justices' seats become vacant… You'll simply go extinct.” Professional members lose their veto under the new judge-selection law.
courts.source: Times of Israel, Jan 4, 2023; JTA, Sep 18, 2026

war.text: Rejected Trump's 15-point plan; no withdrawal “until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.”

wb.text: “As long as I am prime minister, no Palestinian state will arise.” (In July 2025 all Likud ministers urged applying sovereignty.)

names.name: Talik Gvili
names.note: mother of Ran Gvili, the last hostage returned

pledges.text: “A strong right-wing government led by me.”
Petitioned to bar the Joint List; Likud, Shas and UTJ representatives voted to bar the Joint List and Ra'am.
Ben-Gvir will be a senior minister in future government.

quote.text: There is no straight. Yashar is a bluff. There's either left or right… Do you want a Palestinian state? (or) do you want a Jewish state?
quote.speaker: Benjamin Netanyahu

bios.name: Benjamin Netanyahu
bios.text: Born 1949. Prime minister 1996–99, 2009–21 and since December 2022, the longest-serving in Israel's history. The first serving prime minister to face criminal charges in court; his trial opened May 24, 2020, and he asked for a pardon on November 30, 2025 (Al Jazeera, Dec 29, 2022; May 24, 2020; Nov 30, 2025).

who.text: Founded 2012. JTA describes it as a party “that follows the tenets of the banned extremist Kach and its late leader Meir Kahane”; Israel outlawed Kach in 1994.

Led by Itamar Ben-Gvir. It won 6 seats in 2022 inside the Religious Zionism joint list. It left the government in Jan 2025 over the hostage-ceasefire deal; Ben-Gvir was reinstated as national security minister in March 2025.
who.source: JPost, Sep 24, 2026; Times of Israel, Jan 18 and Mar 19, 2025

voters.text: 2022: 6 seats as part of the Religious Zionism joint list (516,470 votes, 10.8%, 14 seats in all).
Draws “traditional Mizrahi voters from the periphery” (Finkelstein).
13% of Haredi first-time voters.
Courting disappointed Likud and Shas voters.

draft.text: Backed the July 14 law banning arrests of draft evaders; proposes Haredi tracks in police and Border Police: “enter service as Haredi and leave it as Haredi.”

courts.text: Ben-Gvir “has supported the government's 2023 judicial reform and opposed efforts to soften the legislation”; Otzma “has sought greater political influence over judicial appointments” (JPost's summary).

war.text: “Disengagement 710” plan: an emigration ministry and 250,000 departures of Palestinians from Gaza a year, NIS 10 billion. “This is a free choice; we are not forcing anyone to leave, but there is encouragement.”

wb.text: Opposes a Palestinian state and evacuating settlers. On Temple Mount prayer: Jews “feel that they are the rightful owners of this place.”

pledges.text: A “fully right-wing government”; no unity with centrists, no Arab parties; demands the Defense or Justice ministry; no Palestinian-state talks.

surplusPartner.text: None signed. Ynet reported Ben-Gvir “not interested” in signing with Ofer Winter.

quote.text: We survived Pharaoh, we will survive Keir Starmer as well.
quote.speaker: Itamar Ben-Gvir, on UK sanctions

bios.name: Itamar Ben-Gvir
bios.text: A self-described disciple of Meir Kahane; convicted in 2007 of incitement to racism and supporting a terrorist organization. National Security Minister from December 2022; left in January 2025 over the Gaza ceasefire and returned in March 2025 (Times of Israel, Sep 15, 2026; Al Jazeera, Mar 18, 2025).

parties.name: Shas
parties.surplusLine: Surplus: UTJ (signed Oct 11; official, CEC gazette Oct 19)

who.text: Founded 1984 as “Shomrei Sefarad” in protest at Agudat Yisrael's thin Sephardi representation, under Rav Ovadia Yosef's Council of Torah Sages. Peak: 17 seats in 1999.
Deri has led it since 2013 (and 1990–99). Former Chief Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef was chosen “to lead” in 2026.

voters.text: Won 28% of Haredi voters and 10.5% of national-religious voters in 2022.
IDI's Malach: “at least three or four Knesset seats' worth of voters who are simply not Haredi.”
First-time voters: 3% overall, 20% of Haredi first-timers.

draft.text: Deri: “The army doesn't want haredi soldiers, get that into your head.” Bill to enshrine Torah study as a basic value.

courts.text: “Fundamentally reform the judicial system and return power to the people and their elected representatives.”

war.text: Supports dismantling Hamas; opposes indefinite Israeli control (JPost's summary).

wb.text: Opposes a Palestinian state; “not central” to its campaign.

relig.text: Orthodox control of marriage, conversion and kashrut; opposes civil marriage and expanded non-Orthodox prayer at the Kotel.

econ.text: Deri: “It is unacceptable that a poor Haredi child would not receive the minimum support as a poor Arab child does.”

names.name: Lt.-Col. (res.) Dror Amos
names.note: Haifa religious council head; 25 years in the IDF

pledges.text: “We support Netanyahu, period.”
Reported plan to sit in opposition until a draft law passes; anonymous source, “not a formal decision.”
“There will be no government in Israel with Shas's support or participation unless the status of yeshiva students is regulated.”

quote.text: Will Bibi Netanyahu repent? Not a chance… Eisenkot, perhaps he will.
quote.speaker: Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef

bios.name: Aryeh Deri
bios.text: Convicted of bribery in 1999 and served 22 months. After a 2022 tax-fraud plea, the High Court ordered him removed as a minister in January 2023 (Al Jazeera, Dec 29, 2022 and Jan 22, 2023; JTA, Feb 14, 2018).

parties.name: UTJ
parties.surplusLine: Surplus: Shas (signed Oct 11; official, CEC gazette Oct 19)

who.text: A joint list of Agudat Yisrael (Hasidic) and Degel HaTorah (Lithuanian) since 1992. Both factions quit the government in July 2025 over the draft.
Sept 5, 2026: Rav Dov Landau removed Gafni and Maklev by letter and made Yaakov Asher head. Sept 8: Porush and Stark formed a third faction inside the list, Homat Torat Yisrael, the first since 1992.

voters.text: 58% of Haredim voted UTJ in 2022; 86% voted UTJ or Shas.
2021: 78% in Modi'in Illit, 60.9% in Bnei Brak.
First-time voters: 9% overall, 45% of Haredi first-timers.

draft.text: “United Torah Judaism, with all its components, will not support or enter any government without regulating the status of Torah learners.”

courts.text: “The Supreme Court has accumulated excessive power.”

wb.text: No unified policy; Agudah leans right, Degel “more moderate.”

relig.text: Same as Shas: Orthodox control of marriage, conversion and kashrut.

pledges.text: No government without a yeshiva-status law, whoever leads it.
Porush's faction requires separate negotiations.
Rav Landau: “We no longer have trust in Netanyahu.”

quote.text: Many things look like etrogim – but this isn't an etrog.
quote.speaker: Yaakov Asher, on Religious Zionism and Otzma courting Haredi voters

bios.name: Yaakov Asher
bios.text: Replaced Moshe Gafni as chairman of Degel HaTorah (Times of Israel, Sep 9, 2026).

bios.name: Yitzhak Goldknopf (no. 2)
bios.text: Leader of UTJ's Agudat Yisrael faction. Resigned as housing minister in June 2025 over the draft of yeshiva students (Times of Israel, Sep 14, 2025; Sep 9, 2026).

parties.name: Religious Zionism–Zehut
parties.surplusLine: Surplus: Likud (signed Oct 6; official, CEC gazette Oct 19)

who.text: The renamed National Union–Tkuma party. Ben-Gvir refused a new joint run: “Smotrich must run in one party and we must run in another party.”
On Sept 1, 2026 formed a “technical bloc” with Moshe Feiglin's Zehut that can separate after the election. Feiglin: “We are a totally separate party.”

voters.text: 2022 (joint list with Otzma and Noam): 516,470 votes, 10.8%, 14 seats; RZ kept 7.
The 2022 joint list took 45% of national-religious voters (up from 30%) and 14% of traditional voters.
Won 22% in settlements vs about 11% nationally.
Settler anger over the draft: “I don't have a political home today.”

draft.text: Most RZ MKs voted for the July 14 law banning arrests of draft evaders. Smotrich: arrests “just make Jews fight one another.”
draft.source: Times of Israel, Jul 14 and Aug 7, 2026

courts.text: “These elections concern the judiciary.” Plan: justices chosen by secret ballot of all judges, AG role split in two, 61-vote override.

war.text: “Return to the whole of Gaza in a big way,” with military rule before sovereignty.

wb.text: E1 approval (~3,400 units) “practically erases the two-state delusion.” 103 new settlements approved during his tenure.
wb.source: Times of Israel, Aug 20, 2025; JPost, Aug 18, 2026

relig.text: “Jewish identity in state institutions and education.”

econ.text: Partner Zehut's platform: a flat tax “as low as possible,” publicly funded school vouchers that parents control, and “thoughtful regulation” of cannabis.

pledges.text: Netanyahu for prime minister; rules out Arab parties.
Would not rule out forming a government with prime ministerial candidate Gadi Eisenkot, but not at the cost of boycotting his partners in the right-wing bloc.

quote.text: Every settlement… is another nail in the coffin of this dangerous idea.
quote.speaker: Bezalel Smotrich, on a Palestinian state

bios.name: Bezalel Smotrich
bios.text: Finance minister, and a minister in the Defense Ministry overseeing Jewish and Palestinian construction in the West Bank's Area C. Said on March 1, 2023 that Huwara “needs to be wiped out.” Sanctioned since June 2025 by the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Norway (Times of Israel, Dec 29, 2022; Al Jazeera, Mar 1, 2023; Jun 10, 2025).

who.text: Amcha Yisrael. Launched Aug 25, 2026 in Jerusalem by Ofer Winter, a retired brigadier general who turned down a Likud slot.
Refused Smotrich's merger offer despite pressure from rabbis. Winter: the public wants “new people.”

voters.text: New list, launched Aug 25, 2026; no 2022 result.
Targets younger voters, reservists, and right-wingers who can't back the current government.

draft.text: “We will not join a government that does not pass, before it is formed, a law that puts an end to draft evasion… Full stop.”

courts.text: An additional judicial tier with a “more balanced” appointment system; remove Bar Association representatives from the Judicial Selection Committee; narrow the “reasonableness” standard.

war.text: “There is one solution in Gaza: migration.”

wb.text: “There will never be a Palestinian state here.”

names.name: Yoseph Haddad
names.note: Arab Orthodox Christian; Golani volunteer wounded in 2006

pledges.text: Recommends only Netanyahu; wants the Defense ministry; won't partner with Bennett or Eisenkot (JPost reports conflict).
Would serve alongside Haredi parties, but not before the draft is settled: “I won't join [a government] until this issue is sorted out.”

surplusPartner.text: None signed. A senior Likud official: “We will not sign with Winter, period.” Ynet reported Ben-Gvir “not interested” in a deal with Winter.

quote.text: New people, those who were not part of the events that led us to October 7.
quote.speaker: Ofer Winter, on what the public wants

bios.name: Ofer Winter
bios.text: Commanded the Givati Brigade, including in the 2014 Gaza war, and the 98th Division; military secretary to Defense Minister Liberman. Left the IDF in 2024 after being passed over for promotion (Times of Israel, Aug 27 and Sep 6, 2026).

parties.name: Noam

who.text: Avi Maoz's party. Won 1 seat in 2022 on the joint slate with Religious Zionism and Otzma Yehudit; filed its own list in 2026.
who.source: Times of Israel, Jul 17, 2025; IDI, accessed Oct 5, 2026

parties.thin: Our research registers have no 2026 profile, polling or bio for Noam or Avi Maoz.

who.text: Founded Sept 16, 2025 by Gadi Eisenkot with about 120 co-founders, after he left the Knesset.
Named for freed hostage Eli Sharabi's line that bringing the captives home was “not about right or left, but straight (yashar).”
Recruits include former Shin Bet chief Yoram Cohen (No. 2), Orit Farkash-Hacohen and Elazar Stern (No. 12).
who.source: Times of Israel, May 5 and Sep 7, 2026

voters.text: New list; no 2022 result. Eisenkot ran in 2022 on National Unity, which won 12 seats.
Targets “Route 4” commuter suburbs: Petah Tikva, Kiryat Ono, Holon; also courting former Likud voters.
voters.source: Times of Israel, Jul 1 and Sep 14, 2026

voters.text: “Security-minded, centrist or moderate-right, secular or religiously traditional.”
Largest share of first-time voters (18–22): 16%.

draft.text: “National Service for All”; deferments capped at 3% of each cohort, about 2,200 people; evaders lose benefits.

courts.text: Repeal the judicial selection law; opposes an override clause; clearer rules for judicial review in a Basic Law.

war.text: “The State of Israel must not accept a reality in which Hamas survives, rearms, and waits.” Wants a state commission of inquiry.

wb.text: Opposes a Palestinian state; would put the Civil Administration back under military coordination.

relig.text: “A secular party, but not anti-religious”; supports civil and same-sex marriage (JC's summary).

econ.text: 15% raise for all conscripts; renter protections; reserve duty capped at 50 days a year.

pledges.text: Partners must accept four principles, including service for all and Hamas “to be dismantled and destroyed.” “I do not rule out any Zionist party.”
On Ra'am: Mansour Abbas “won't be part of my next government.” No Haredi party currently meets his criteria.
"Absolutely not. I will not serve under Netanyahu, not even in a rotation agreement." (Jerusalem Post, Oct 21, 2026)

quote.text: Netanyahu initially opposed including that objective, and I forced it upon him on the ninth day of the war.
quote.speaker: Gadi Eisenkot, on making the hostages a war goal

bios.name: Gadi Eisenkot
bios.text: Son of immigrants from Morocco; grew up in Tiberias and Eilat. Rose through the Golani Brigade; IDF Chief of Staff until 2019. His son Gal was killed in Gaza in December 2023. JTA: he would be Israel's first Mizrahi prime minister (JTA, Sep 9, 2026).

who.text: “Together – Led by Bennett.” Yesh Atid runs inside this list under a deal signed Apr 25–26, 2026; Lapid is no. 2 and Yesh Atid holds 10 of the top 24 slots. Not a formal merger.
Polling fell from about 25 seats in May to roughly half; the list has tacked toward the liberal-Zionist center.

voters.text: 2022: Yesh Atid 847,435 votes, 17.8%, 24 seats; Bennett did not run.
Yesh Atid's 2022 voters were 78.5% secular, 20% traditional; it took 39% of the secular vote.
Russian speakers: Bennett 17%.
First-time voters: 10%.

draft.text: Bennett: “Bibi is talking about a 50% exemption, Gadi is talking about a 30% exemption, I am talking about 0 exemption.” End stipends for married yeshiva students.

courts.text: A Basic Law on how Basic Laws are made and when courts may step in; repeal the judicial appointments law; 8-year term limits for prime ministers.

war.text: “We must not budge a centimeter from the red line until Hamas is disarmed.” Supports a state commission on Oct 7.

wb.text: Opposes a Palestinian state “under any constellation”; backs E1; would dismantle illegal outposts while backing “legal settlement in Area C.”
wb.source: JPost, Aug 30; Times of Israel, Jun 23, 2026

relig.text: Civil marriage; cities choose on Shabbat transit; “full equality of rights to protect the LGBTQ community.”

econ.text: “We will cut food prices by 30% within three years.”

pledges.text: Zionist parties only: no Arab or Haredi parties; “no compromises on draft issues.”
Will rely only on Zionist parties for his coalition, not on Ra'am again: an explicit break from his 2021 government.

quote.text: I'm a right-wing guy, I'm not changing my opinions. But I'm not a schmuck.
quote.speaker: Naftali Bennett

bios.name: Naftali Bennett
bios.text: Born in Haifa to American immigrants. Co-founded the fraud-detection firm Cyota and directed the Yesha Council. Prime minister June 2021–June 2022, the first to regularly wear a kippah (JTA, Jun 1, 2021).

bios.name: Yair Lapid (no. 2)
bios.text: A former TV journalist who founded Yesh Atid in 2012; it became the Knesset's second-largest party in 2013. Prime minister July–December 2022, then opposition leader (JTA, Mar 2, 2015; Jul 1, 2022).

who.text: Labor (founded 1968; prime ministers Meir, Rabin, Peres) and Meretz (1992) running together. A partial merger: both keep their own institutions.
Yair Golan won Labor's leadership in May 2024 with 95% of the vote. The 2026 slate includes anti-government protest leader Moshe Radman and former Meretz MK Gaby Lasky.

voters.text: 2022: Labor 175,992 votes, 3.7%, 4 seats; Meretz 150,793, 3.2%, 0 seats (its first time out of the Knesset).
Labor and Meretz took 16% of the secular vote in 2022, down from 19%.
First-time voters: 7%. Claims more than 100,000 members.

draft.text: Universal service “within a national and equal framework.” Golan has called mass Haredi conscription “impractical.”
draft.source: Ynet, Sep 16; Times of Israel, Aug 5, 2026

courts.text: Urgent problems are “delays, overloaded courts and a shortage of judges”; an intermediate appeals court; opposes the 2023 reform.

wb.text: Opposes annexation; defund outposts. Golan: civil separation with Israeli security control.

relig.text: Civil marriage; limited Shabbat public transport in secular towns; amend the Nation-State Law.

econ.text: “Reduce living costs, improve social services, rebuild the public sector”; JPost calls the detail “less clearly defined.”

pledges.text: No Haredi parties: “the Haredim will be outside [the government], that is a guarantee.” Golan said this after a leaked clip in which he would back a government that needed a Haredi party “provided that Likud, Smotrich, and Ben Gvir are not there.”
Open to an Arab party: “It is natural, right, appropriate and democratic” (the party says this is its own platform, not the bloc's).
pledges.source: Kan via Times of Israel, Sep 27, 2026

quote.text: In our government, there will be zero criminal defendants. Zero.
quote.speaker: Yair Golan

bios.name: Yair Golan
bios.text: A former IDF deputy chief of staff. On October 7 he drove to the Nova festival area and rescued people. Won Labor's leadership in May 2024 with 95% of the vote (Times of Israel, May 28, 2024; Sep 10, 2026).

parties.name: Yisrael Beiteinu

who.text: Founded 1999 by Avigdor Liberman; first aimed at Soviet immigrants, later “right-wing secular voters.” Peak: 15 seats in 2009.
In 2019 Liberman “opposed any compromise regarding the draft law,” which sank coalition talks and forced a repeat election.

voters.text: Russian speakers: Yisrael Beiteinu 23%; 94% of them back a universal draft.
First-time voters: 6%.

draft.text: Everyone at 18: “Jews, Muslims, Christians, Druze and Circassians”; sanctions including travel bans.

courts.text: A written constitution put to a national referendum; amendments would need 80 MKs.

war.text: Board of Peace arrangements are “a capitulation to terror.” A state commission on Oct 7 is a condition.
war.source: JPost, Aug 12; Times of Israel, Aug 17, 2026

relig.text: Civil marriage and divorce; a Western Wall compromise; local choice on Shabbat transit; a mandatory core curriculum.

names.name: Sharon Sharabi
names.note: brother of freed hostage Eli Sharabi

parties.namesSource: JPost and Times of Israel, Sep 6, 2026

pledges.text: No Netanyahu, no Arab parties, no Haredi parties: “not for the Arab parties and not for the haredi parties.”
pledges.source: JPost, Sep 21, 2025; Times of Israel, Oct 3, 2026

pledges.text: Conditions: Oct 7 inquiry, universal service, prime-minister term limits, core curriculum, constitution by referendum.

quote.text: We are the Likud of yesteryear.
quote.speaker: Yisrael Beiteinu slogan

bios.name: Avigdor Liberman
bios.text: Born in what is now Moldova; immigrated in 1978 at 19. Founded Yisrael Beiteinu in 1999. In 2019 his refusal to join Netanyahu's government over the Haredi draft law forced a second election that year (JTA, Jun 6, 2019).

parties.name: Blue and White
parties.status: Below threshold in every recent poll

who.text: Down to 3 MKs after defections. Gantz will drop out in the last week if the party is not crossing the threshold.

parties.thin: Our party registers do not profile Blue and White beyond this.

bios.name: Benny Gantz
bios.text: Son of Holocaust survivors; IDF Chief of Staff. Chaired Blue and White; alternate prime minister in 2020. Left the war cabinet June 9, 2024 (JTA, Jan 27, 2021; Jun 10, 2024).

who.text: Yoaz Hendel founded The Reservists on Sept 18, 2025. On Sept 6, 2026, two days before the slate deadline, he joined forces with Yaron Zelekha's Economic Party.
Pitches itself as a “third bloc.” Its bloc is disputed: IsraelEd says it would join Netanyahu; Times of Israel calls it non-aligned.

voters.text: New list; no 2022 seats. Zelekha's party won 0.29% (13,920 votes) in 2022.

Hendel: “Those wanting government with ultra-Orthodox parties know who to vote for… Those comfortable with minority government relying on Arab parties have their opposition choice. We must provide the alternative.”
First crossed the threshold in Channel 13's polling on Sept 23, 2026, with 4 seats.

draft.text: “Those who do not serve cannot vote or be elected to the Knesset.” A draft law must pass before a government is sworn in.

courts.text: First a Basic Law on legislation, with a new, balanced Judicial Selection Committee; a Knesset override only with more than 72 MKs. Its platform limits a prime minister to eight years or two terms.

war.text: Hendel earlier proposed moving about 1.5 million Palestinians from Gaza to “a tent city outside the Strip”; Wilf backs a “voluntary emigration directorate for Gaza.”

wb.text: “We support settlement throughout all parts of the State of Israel.” Platform: “We will act to prevent a Palestinian state through diplomatic and political channels.”

econ.text: Zelekha joined promising to fight “tycoons and the cost of living”; the platform pledges “a fight against monopolies” to increase competition and lower living costs.

pledges.text: A “Zionist unity government without Arab or Haredi parties”; supports a state commission of inquiry.
pledges.source: Times of Israel, Nov 20, 2025; Ynet, Oct 4, 2026

pledges.text: On Netanyahu, mixed: “Netanyahu is not my red line” (Aug 11) vs. “whoever is responsible for October 7 needs to go home, and that includes Netanyahu” (Aug 23).

surplusPartner.text: None signed. Hendel offered Ofer Winter a surplus deal; Winter did not respond.

quote.text: Our mission is solely to establish a Zionist government.
quote.speaker: The Reservists

bios.name: Yoaz Hendel
bios.text: A political scientist, former Netanyahu aide and battalion commander in the IDF reserves. Entered politics with Blue and White in 2019; later communications minister (Times of Israel, Sep 18, 2025; Aug 6, 2026).

who.text: First formed in 2015 by all four Arab-led parties (13 seats; peak of 15 in 2020). Re-formed Aug 19, 2026 as Hadash–Ta'al–Balad, without Ra'am.

Hadash, the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, sums itself up as “Democracy. Peace. Equality.” and lists first “a just, comprehensive and stable Israeli-Palestinian and Israeli-Arab peace.” The Jerusalem Post: Hadash “has historically emphasized Jewish-Arab partnership.”

Under Basic Law: The Knesset, Section 7A, a list or candidate can be barred for negating Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, inciting racism, or supporting armed struggle against Israel. On Likud's petition the Central Elections Committee voted Sept 23 to bar the list, 18–5; the Supreme Court reinstated it unanimously on Oct 2.

Ofer Cassif (No. 6) was barred 19–5, with two abstentions (the Jerusalem Post's count; Al Jazeera, citing Adalah, reported 18–5), on Likud's petition, for negating Israel as a Jewish and democratic state and supporting armed struggle. Likud's lawyer cited Cassif's accusations against Israel over the war in Gaza and, in the Post's words, his “support for international proceedings and sanctions, calls for boycotts and statements about Palestinian resistance”; Cassif said he had “expressly said he opposed violence and supported nonviolent struggle.” The Supreme Court reinstated him 7–2 (Justices Mintz and Stein dissenting): the evidence had not reached the required “critical mass.”
who.source: JPost, Oct 1 and Oct 2, 2026; Al Jazeera, Sep 26, 2026

who.text: No. 3 Sami Abu Shehadeh (Balad) was barred 31–4 on Otzma Yehudit's petition, for supporting armed struggle against Israel, over an article he published on Oct 8, 2023. He withdrew after the court's president told him there was “a majority on the bench to bar” him.
who.source: JPost, Oct 1 and Oct 2, 2026; Ynet, Oct 2, 2026; Times of Israel, Oct 2, 2026

voters.text: 2022 (ran split): Hadash–Ta'al 178,735 votes, 3.8%, 5 seats; Balad 138,617, 2.9%, 0 seats.
In Arab and Druze towns in 2022: Hadash–Ta'al 28.8%, Balad 21.7%. Arab turnout 53.2%.
77.2% of Arab citizens support an Arab party joining the government.

draft.text: Opposes drafting Haredi men or any form of compulsory enlistment: “sanctions should not be imposed on someone who chooses not to enlist.”

courts.text: Supports reforms that strengthen democratic protections and safeguard the rights of all citizens, particularly minority communities; an appointment mechanism that preserves judicial independence.

war.text: “End Gaza destruction and West Bank ethnic cleansing.”

wb.text: Jabareen: renewed negotiations toward “a Palestinian state alongside Israel.”

relig.text: “Full civic and national equality for Arab citizens.”

econ.text: Jabareen: the list would seek “action against organized crime, and increased budgets for Arab society and local authorities” (the Post's summary).

pledges.text: Won't join Netanyahu.
Conditions for backing an Eisenkot bloc: equality, a development plan, real action on crime, “a clear position against settlements”; did not rule out “a parliamentary safety net.”

quote.text: A political, racist, and anti-democratic decision… an attempt to exclude the political representation of more than one million voters.
quote.speaker: The Joint List, on the committee's vote to bar it

bios.name: Yousef Jabareen
bios.text: From Umm al-Fahm; a legal scholar. MK 2015–21. Elected Hadash chair May 16, 2026 with 82%, replacing Ayman Odeh, who had led it since 2015 and did not seek reelection (Times of Israel, May 16, 2026).

bios.name: Ahmad Tibi (no. 2)
bios.text: Longtime chairman of Ta'al; No. 2 on the Joint List (Times of Israel, Sep 20, 2026).

who.text: Founded in 1996; rooted in the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement. In 2021 it became the first Arab party to formally join an Israeli governing coalition.
In Dec 2025 Abbas said Ra'am was becoming “a completely civic party, with separate institutions,” cutting ties with the Islamic Shura Council: “we are not a part of the Muslim Brotherhood.”
Barred by the Elections Committee Sept 23, 18–5; reinstated unanimously by the Supreme Court Oct 2.
who.source: Times of Israel, Sep 23; JPost, Oct 1 and Oct 2, 2026

voters.text: Took 35.2% of the Arab and Druze vote in 2022, and 73.9% in the Negev.
Strongholds: the Negev and the Triangle; now seeking Christian and Druze voters, with a 7–8 seat target.

draft.text: Opposes a draft law that would require young Arab citizens to serve in the IDF or perform civilian service; declined to respond on Haredi enlistment.

courts.text: Declined to give a current position on the judicial overhaul; in 2023 Abbas said “no branch of government should hold absolute power.”

war.text: Abbas, Dec 2023: Palestinian armed groups “need to throw down their arms” and work with the Palestinian Authority toward “a state of Palestine in a peaceful solution alongside the state of Israel.” Ra'am in 2026 on Oct 7: there is “a need for a comprehensive, independent and impartial investigation.”
war.source: Times of Israel, Dec 3, 2023; Ynet, Oct 4, 2026

wb.text: Abbas: a Palestinian state is “a reality, which most of the world recognizes, with the exception of the United States and Israel. We want them to recognize it, and we'll work to achieve peace.” Supports a negotiated two-state solution; opposes extending Israeli sovereignty.
wb.source: Times of Israel, Aug 22, 2026; Ynet, Sep 30, 2026

relig.text: Earlier: “Israel was born as a Jewish state, and it will remain so.” The AG told the committee Abbas recognizes Israel's Jewish character.

econ.text: Budgets, planning, housing and jobs for Arab towns; seeks the violence and crime portfolio. No full manifesto.

names.name: Yoav Segalovitz
names.note: Jewish former police commander; joined Aug 31

names.name: Walid Taha
names.note: on the Aug 22 slate; final slot not confirmed

pledges.text: Open to any coalition, including one led by Likud.
Eisenkot said Sept 26 that Abbas “won't be part of my next government.” Segalovitz: “Eisenkot won't have a government without Ra'am.”

quote.text: I am going to an Arab party. They are not coming to me.
quote.speaker: Yoav Segalovitz

bios.name: Mansour Abbas
bios.text: Ra'am chair; the first leader of a majority-Arab party to join an Israeli government, in 2021 (JTA, Jul 19, 2022).

bios.name: Yoav Segalovitz (no. 2)
bios.text: Jewish, 67. Founded and commanded the police's Lahav 433 unit and headed its Investigations and Intelligence Division; deputy public security minister 2021–22. Second on Ra'am's slate (Times of Israel, Aug 16, Aug 31 and Sep 17, 2026).

results.agreementsNote: Seat estimates use the five surplus-vote agreements the Central Elections Committee published in the Official Gazette on Oct 19, 2026 (Yalkut HaPirsumim 15045, p. 1098): Yashar–The Democrats, B'Yachad–Yisrael Beiteinu, Joint List–Ra'am, Likud–Religious Zionism, Shas–UTJ. A sixth pair of fringe lists is not modelled. Otzma Yehudit, Amcha Yisrael, the Reservists, Blue and White and Noam filed none. Verified against the gazette Oct 23.

calibration.about: Final-week polls against results, Netanyahu-aligned bloc, every election under the 3.25% threshold. 'field' is the mean of the final poll of each firm other than Direct Polls / Shlomo Filber's firms; 'directPolls' is that firm's final poll where it published one in the final week. Source: Wikipedia opinion-polling pages for each election, read 2026-10-23. Bloc definitions follow the tables: 2015 Likud+Jewish Home+Shas+UTJ+Yisrael Beiteinu+Yachad; Apr 2019 the right bloc incl. Kulanu and YB; Sep 2019 and Mar 2020 Likud+Shas+UTJ+Yamina; 2021 Likud+Shas+UTJ+RZ; 2022 Likud+Shas+UTJ+RZ. 'shasError' is Shas's own seat miss (result minus final-week polls) in the same election, from round1/B-list-bias.md; kept for the record: taking the lean net of it was tested in backtest/v2.mjs and rejected (it turns the leave-future-out lean negative and under-predicts the bloc by 3 seats).

thresholdLists.about: Lists shown at 4-5 seats by most final-week polls, and whether they passed.

perListError.about: theMadad, 2022: mean absolute error per list in polls 0-14 days before the vote.

listPriors.about: Vote-share points added to the field mean before the lean, each a class of list the final-week polls have missed in one direction in both halves of 2013-2022 (round1/B-list-bias.md; the direction confirmed independently in round1/C-threshold.md and round1/E-context.md). Shrunk 20-40% toward zero. The common lean stays gross: netting it of the Shas miss scored worse out of sample (backtest/v2.mjs). Version 3 (round2/B): the Joint List's +0.4 is superseded by the Arab sector turnout term below (sectorTurnout.replacesPriors) and kept here only so version 2 can be reproduced (model.mjs opts.v2).

withdrawn.about: Lists that left the race after the ballot was set; still on the ballot, their votes are wasted. Dropped from the model, their polled share folded into the fringe.

lists.source: Times of Israel, Oct 19, 2026: Gantz withdraws Blue and White

fringe.about: Share of the vote going to lists the polls do not report separately, held out of every modelled list's share and counted in the threshold's denominator. 0.4-1.5% in 2013-2022; 1.8% for 2026 from the polls' own printed shares of the small lists outside the 15 modelled (Haredi Public about 0.7%, Noam about 0.5%, others 0.3-0.5%; round2/H-context.md section 5). 1.5% in version 2; neutral on the backtest either way.

smallList.about: Final-field misses of lists polled at 2-5%, 2015-2022 (round2/C-threshold-swing.md): Gaussian, sd 0.98 net of the class priors (90% cluster bootstrap 0.71-1.29; 0.91 with 2013), no skew once Blue and White 2021 is set aside, no dependence on the distance from the line or on the final-week trend, no strategic desertion keyed to the line. First-time and first-solo small lists -0.75 (9 cases, 8 negative; 90% -1.16 to -0.20): listPriors keeps -0.8. unprintedBelowShare is the last-resort share for a list a poll prints below the threshold with no percentage, when the outlet printed none in the window and no other current poll did: 2.5%, the median printed share (2015-2022) of such lists that other polls showed passing; 2% in version 2 was below 38 of those 51 figures. It decided no call in the record.

arabSwing.about: RMS of the Arab lists' bloc miss in 2020-22, +1.0, -1.7, +2.0 seats: a turnout swing of their own (round1/F-review.md F5, round1/E-context.md 2.2).

windowDays.about: One latest poll per outlet within this many days of the newest; in 2019-22 the latest poll per firm beat every rule that let older polls back in (round1/D-pollsters.md 3).

sectorTurnout.about: Round 2, memo B (round2/B-sector-turnout.md): the polls behave as if anchored on the previous election's Arab-sector turnout; the change in the Arab list-vote index I = Arab turnout x loyalty to Arab lists / general turnout explains about 90% of the Arab lists' final-poll miss in hindsight (R2 0.91, 2013-2022) and, forecast by mean reversion of I (stationary around 0.65 since 1999), beats the fixed priors leave-future-out (sector MAE 0.54 vs 1.14 points; per-list seat error 1.32 vs 1.36, a noise-sized margin). The term is carried by the Joint List (Ra'am keeps its +0.6 class prior: scaling it too pushes it under the threshold in Apr 2019 and 2021). logShift is the history-only centre for 2026: 2022's I sat at its long-run mean, so the expected change is nil (0.008); sdLog 0.196 is the carrier list's spread. Memo B's alternative, centring 2026 Arab turnout at 57% (logShift 0.072), was not taken: memo H finds version 2 already at the pre-blackout turnout consensus. Replaces listPriors.jl and arabSwing for the carrier lists. Backtest values are derived leave-future-out in scripts/forecast/round2/B/common.mjs.

swing.about: Version 3 (round2/G-uncertainty.md): the Netanyahu-bloc swing is lean + max(1.5, resid x sqrt(1 + 1/n)) x t(max(3, n - 1)) seats, the predictive distribution of the next miss from n past elections; for 2026 scale 1.65, 5 degrees of freedom, sd 2.1. Version 2's N(0, max(3, 2 x resid)) = N(0, 3.1) put all six past results between the 31st and 66th percentiles (probability about 0.003 if calibrated). Leave-future-out the change leaves per-list error identical and improves majority Brier 0.090 to 0.054 and list CRPS 2.165 to 2.137. The bloc point is the median of the simulated bloc total (Netanyahu-bloc error 1.94 to 1.33 under every seed).
